content: Ferric oxide, also known as iron(III) oxide, is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Fe₂O₃. It is one of the three primary oxides of iron, alongside iron(II) oxide (FeO), which is relatively rare, and iron(II,III) oxide (Fe₃O₄), which naturally occurs as the mineral magnetite. Fe₂O₃ is commonly found in nature as the mineral hematite, which serves as the primary source of iron for the steel industry. This compound is ferrimagnetic, dark red in color, and reacts readily with acids. While often referred to as rust, this term is somewhat imprecise in a chemical context, as rust is better described as hydrated ferric oxide, a poorly defined material. Fe₂O₃ exists in several polymorphic forms, with the two main ones being the alpha (α) and gamma (γ) phases. In both forms, iron atoms are coordinated octahedrally, meaning each iron atom is surrounded by six oxygen atoms. The alpha phase (α-Fe₂O₃) has a rhombohedral crystal structure similar to corundum (α-Al₂O₃) and is the most common form. It naturally occurs as hematite, the primary iron ore. This phase is antiferromagnetic below approximately 260 K (the Morin transition temperature) and exhibits weak ferromagnetism between 260 K and its Néel temperature of 950 K. It can be synthesized through thermal decomposition or precipitation in the liquid phase. The gamma phase (γ-Fe₂O₃) has a cubic crystal structure and is metastable, converting to the alpha phase at high temperatures. It naturally occurs as the mineral maghemite. This phase is ferromagnetic and is used in applications such as magnetic recording tapes. However, ultrafine particles of γ-Fe₂O₃ smaller than 10 nanometers exhibit superparamagnetic behavior. It can be prepared by thermal dehydration of gamma iron(III) oxide-hydroxide or by careful oxidation of iron(II,III) oxide (Fe₃O₄). Ultrafine particles can also be synthesized via thermal decomposition of iron(III) oxalate. Other less common phases of Fe₂O₃ include the beta (β) and epsilon (ε) phases. The β-phase has a cubic body-centered structure and is metastable, converting to the alpha phase above 500°C. It can be prepared by reducing hematite with carbon, pyrolyzing iron(III) chloride solutions, or thermally decomposing iron(III) sulfate. The ε-phase has a rhombic structure and exhibits magnetic properties intermediate between the alpha and gamma phases. However, obtaining a pure ε-phase is challenging due to contamination with the alpha and gamma phases. It can be prepared by thermal transformation of the gamma phase or by oxidation of iron in an electric arc. Additionally, an amorphous form of Fe₂O₃ has been reported under high-pressure conditions. Hydrated forms of iron(III) oxide also exist. When an alkali is added to solutions of soluble Fe(III) salts, a red-brown gelatinous precipitate forms, which is not Fe(OH)₃ but rather Fe₂O₃·H₂O (also written as Fe(O)OH). Various hydrated forms, such as lepidocrocite (γ-Fe(O)OH) and goethite, are found in rust. Heating Fe₂O₃·H₂O results in the loss of water, and further heating at 1670 K converts Fe₂O₃ to black Fe₃O₄ (magnetite). Fe(O)OH dissolves in acids, releasing Fe³⁺ ions, and in concentrated aqueous alkali, Fe₂O₃ forms ferrate ions (FeO₄³⁻). The most significant reaction involving Fe₂O₃ is its carbothermal reduction, which produces iron for steelmaking. Another notable reaction is the highly exothermic thermite reaction with aluminum, used for welding thick metals like train tracks and in weaponry. Fe₂O₃ also reacts with acids such as hydrochloric and sulfuric acids and dissolves in chelating agents like EDTA and oxalic acid. Heating Fe₂O₃ with other metal oxides or carbonates yields ferrates. Ferric oxide can be synthesized in the laboratory by electrolyzing a sodium bicarbonate solution with an iron anode, producing hydrated iron(III) oxide, which dehydrates around 200°C. It can also be prepared by thermally decomposing iron(III) hydroxide above 200°C. A finely powdered form of ferric oxide, known as jeweler's rouge or red rouge, is used for polishing metallic jewelry and lenses. It is also historically used as a cosmetic. Rouge provides a superior finish compared to modern polishes like cerium(IV) oxide and is still used in optics and jewelry fabrication. It is available as a powder, paste, or solid bar and is often applied to leather strops for sharpening edged tools. Iron(III) oxide is also used as a pigment under names like Pigment Brown 6, Pigment Brown 7, and Pigment Red 101. Some of these pigments, such as Pigment Red 101, are FDA-approved for use in cosmetics. Iron oxides are also used as pigments in dental composites alongside titanium oxides. Hematite is the characteristic component of the Swedish paint color Falu red. In magnetic recording, iron(III) oxide was historically the most common magnetic particle used in storage media such as magnetic disks and tapes. However, modern magnetic storage media, particularly hard disk drives, now use advanced thin-film technology with multiple layers. The alpha phase of Fe₂O₃ has been studied for over 25 years as a photoanode in water-splitting reactions. Additionally, a 5% iron(III) oxide formulation is known as calamine, the active ingredient in calamine lotion.
